def kth_inversion_permutation(n, k, t):
    """Return the t-th permutation of 1..n, in lexicographic order, among all
    permutations that have exactly k inversions.

    An inversion of a permutation p (0-indexed here for clarity) is a pair of
    positions (i, j) with i < j and p[i] > p[j].  The candidates are ALL
    permutations of the integers 1..n whose inversion count is exactly k;
    they are ordered lexicographically as integer sequences, and the t-th one
    (1-indexed) must be returned as a list of ints.

    If there are fewer than t such permutations -- including the case where k
    exceeds the maximum possible inversion count n*(n-1)//2, so no candidate
    exists at all -- return the empty list [].

    Input domain: 1 <= n <= 50, 0 <= k <= 2000, 1 <= t <= 10**18, all ints.
    (Note: the number of candidate permutations can be astronomically larger
    than 10**18, and n = 50 has 50! ~ 3*10**64 permutations in total, so any
    form of enumeration is hopeless; the intended solution is exact and runs
    in well under 0.1 seconds.)

    Output: a list of n distinct ints (a permutation of 1..n), or [] as
    specified above.  There are no other tie-breaks: the permutation with
    exactly k inversions that is t-th in lexicographic order is unique.

    >>> kth_inversion_permutation(3, 1, 1)
    [1, 3, 2]
    >>> kth_inversion_permutation(4, 2, 3)
    [2, 1, 4, 3]
    >>> kth_inversion_permutation(3, 1, 5)
    []
    """
